title: Identity providers
intro: Single sign-on and the protocols behind it (OIDC, OAuth 2.0, SAML, LDAP, Kerberos, SCIM), the open source identity providers, and how Argo CD and Kubernetes use one.
scope: Open source or free to use. Paid products are left out unless they are a CNCF alternative. The three cloud services are references you asked for, and are marked as not open source.

groups.label: Concepts and protocols
groups.about: What single sign-on is and the standards behind it.

groups.label: Directories and Kerberos
groups.about: Where users are stored, and ticket based login.

groups.label: Cloud identity services
groups.about: Managed services, as references. They are not open source.

groups.label: GitOps and Kubernetes
groups.about: How Argo CD and the Kubernetes API server use an identity provider.

entries.name: SSO and federation
entries.summary: One login for many applications. An identity provider authenticates the user once and tells each application who they are, using a protocol such as OIDC or SAML.

cncf.text: A concept, not a project.

version.name: Concept (protocol versions: OIDC Core 1.0, SAML 2.0)
version.docs: Specifications and product docs listed in Sources

notes: This is a summary of the protocol entries, not a source of its own. How single logout works in practice differs per product and is not covered here (unconfirmed).

sections.title: Terms
items: Identity provider (IdP): authenticates the user and vouches for them to applications. In SAML the applications are service providers (SP). SAML calls the IdP and SP an asserting party and a relying party.
In OpenID Connect the application is the client, which asks the server to authenticate a user and gets an ID Token (a JWT) back.

Federation: an application trusts an identity provider run by someone else, so the user does not need an account at each application. Keycloak and Dex both do this as brokers: they sit between the application and other identity providers.

sections.title: Which protocol does what
items: OpenID Connect: login for web, mobile and API clients. An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. Tokens are JSON.
SAML 2.0: login, mostly browser based. XML assertions signed with XML Signature.
OAuth 2.0 alone: delegated access to an API. It says what a client may do, not who the user is.
LDAP: reading and checking users in a directory (bind, search). It is not a web login protocol by itself, but many identity providers use a directory as their user store.
Kerberos: ticket based login inside a network realm.
SCIM: creating and updating user and group accounts in other systems. It does not log anyone in.

sections.title: Typical setup
items: One identity provider holds or federates the users. Each application is registered with it: a client in OIDC, a service provider with metadata in SAML.
The identity provider reads users from a directory (LDAP or Active Directory in Keycloak's case) or from other identity providers.
Add multi-factor authentication and the group or role claims in one place, the identity provider, instead of in every application.
Platforms that run other people's apps, such as Argo CD and Kubernetes, accept OIDC. See Argo CD and Kubernetes.

entries.name: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
entries.summary: An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. The client sends the user to the provider, then receives an ID Token (a signed JWT) that says who logged in.

started.basis: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 first final, per the spec's status text

cncf.text: Specified by the OpenID Foundation, not a CNCF project.

compare.text: OIDC uses JSON and JWT over HTTP and fits APIs, mobile and single page apps. SAML uses XML assertions and is mostly for browser login.
OAuth 2.0 grants access to an API. OIDC adds the ID Token and the openid scope to say who the user is.

notes: The spec page was read for the first 100,000 of 285,816 characters. The standard scopes beyond openid (profile, email, address, phone, offline_access) were not on the part read, so they are not listed here (unconfirmed).
Start date: the spec status text says the original Final was February 2014. Whether that is the first publication is unconfirmed.

sections.title: What it is
items: OpenID Connect 1.0 is "a simple identity layer on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol". It is built on OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) and ID Tokens are JSON Web Tokens.
A request is an OpenID Connect request only if it includes the scope openid.
The provider's endpoints (authorization, token) are normally found through OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0. Client registration is a separate specification, Dynamic Client Registration 1.0.

sections.title: Flows
items: Authorization Code Flow: response_type code. The client gets a code in the redirect and exchanges it at the token endpoint. This is the flow RFC 9700 prefers.

Implicit Flow: response_type id_token or id_token token. Tokens come back in the redirect. RFC 9700 says clients should not use response types that issue access tokens in the authorization response unless token injection is prevented.
Hybrid Flow: response_type code id_token, code token or code id_token token.

sections.title: ID Token and UserInfo
items: Required ID Token claims: iss (issuer), sub (subject), aud (audience), exp (expiry), iat (issued at). nonce, auth_time and acr are conditional or optional.
The UserInfo endpoint is a protected resource that returns claims about the user when given an access token. Its URL must use https.
The client must check the ID Token, in particular that aud contains its own client id and that it is not expired. A recipient that does not find itself in aud must reject a JWT (RFC 7519).

sections.title: Security practice (from RFC 9700, January 2025)
items: Public clients must use PKCE and authorization servers must support it. S256 is the only challenge method that does not expose the verifier in the authorization request.
Redirect URIs are matched by exact string comparison, except the port of a localhost redirect for native apps.
The resource owner password credentials grant must not be used.
Refresh tokens for public clients must be sender-constrained or rotated.

entries.name: OAuth 2.0
entries.summary: An authorization framework: a client gets an access token from an authorization server to call an API for a user. Not a login protocol by itself.

cncf.text: Specified by the IETF, not a CNCF project.

notes: RFC 6749 is dated October 2012; the day is not on the page read. OAuth 2.1 is not covered: its status was not checked (unconfirmed).
RFC 9700 date is January 2025, as shown on the page; the day is not.
version.released is set to the first day of the month of RFC 9700, because the page shows only the month.

sections.title: Model
items: Roles: resource owner, resource server, client, authorization server.
Endpoints: the authorization endpoint (user agent redirect) and the token endpoint (exchange a grant for an access token).
Client types: confidential (can keep a secret, such as a server application) and public (cannot, such as a browser or native app).
Tokens: an access token is a scoped, time limited credential for the resource server. A refresh token only goes to the authorization server, to get new access tokens. Issuing one is optional.

sections.title: Grants
items: RFC 6749 defines four: authorization code, implicit, resource owner password credentials, client credentials.
RFC 9700 (January 2025, updates RFC 6749) says to prefer authorization code with PKCE, not to use the password grant, and to avoid implicit.

entries.name: JSON Web Token (JWT)
entries.summary: A compact signed (or encrypted) set of claims. ID Tokens in OIDC are JWTs.

cncf.text: Specified by the IETF, not a CNCF project.

notes: RFC 7519 is dated May 2015; the day is not on the page. version.released is the first of that month.

sections.title: Structure
items: A signed JWT in compact form has three base64url parts separated by periods: header, payload (the claims) and signature. A JWT can instead be encrypted as a JWE.
Registered claims, none mandatory: iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti. A recipient that does not find itself in aud must reject the token.

sections.title: Care
items: The spec allows unsecured JWTs with alg none. It says which algorithms are accepted is an application decision, so a verifier should accept only the algorithms it expects.
RFC 8725 and RFC 7797 later updated RFC 7519.

entries.name: SAML 2.0
entries.summary: An OASIS standard that carries authentication, attribute and authorization statements as XML assertions between an identity provider and a service provider. Mostly browser single sign-on.

started.basis: SAML 2.0 core specs (assertions and protocols), per the technical overview

cncf.text: Specified by OASIS, not a CNCF project.

compare.text: SAML is XML and browser focused, older (2005). OIDC is JSON and also suits APIs and native apps.

notes: The overview page is a Committee Draft 02 dated 25 March 2008. It states that the core Assertions and Protocols specifications are dated March 2005. The final OASIS standard text itself was not read (unconfirmed).
Start date is the month of the core specifications, as stated in the overview.

sections.title: Roles and statements
items: An asserting party (SAML authority) makes assertions and a relying party uses them. In web single sign-on these are the identity provider (IdP) and the service provider (SP). The principal (subject) is usually the user.
An assertion holds three kinds of statements: authentication, attribute and authorization decision.

sections.title: Protocols, bindings, profiles
items: Protocols: Authentication Request, Single Logout, Assertion Query and Request, Artifact Resolution, Name Identifier Management, Name Identifier Mapping.
Bindings (how messages travel): HTTP Redirect, HTTP POST, HTTP Artifact, SOAP, Reverse SOAP (PAOS), URI.
Profiles: Web Browser SSO, Enhanced Client or Proxy (ECP), Identity Provider Discovery, Single Logout.

sections.title: Login flows and trust
items: SP-initiated: the user starts at the SP, which sends an authentication request to the IdP and gets an assertion back.
IdP-initiated: the user starts at the IdP, which sends an assertion to the SP without a prior request.
Metadata is an XML document describing an entity: endpoints, supported bindings, roles, signing and encryption keys. Partners exchange it to set up trust.
An assertion delivered through the browser with the HTTP POST binding must be signed with XML Signature.

entries.name: SCIM 2.0
entries.summary: A REST protocol and schema for creating and updating users and groups in other systems. It provisions accounts, it does not log anyone in.

cncf.text: Specified by the IETF, not a CNCF project.

notes: RFC 7644 is dated September 2015; the day is not on the page. version.released is the first of that month.

sections.title: Protocol
items: HTTP methods: GET reads, POST creates and also carries search and bulk requests, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part of a resource, DELETE removes. PUT must not be used to create.
Endpoints: /Users, /Groups, /Me, /ServiceProviderConfig, /ResourceTypes, /Schemas, /Bulk, /.search.
Filters use operators such as eq, ne, co, sw, ew, pr, gt, le, combined with and, or, not. Servers may choose not to support filtering. PATCH is optional, PUT must be supported.
SCIM defines no authentication of its own. It relies on TLS and standard HTTP authentication, such as OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens. Basic authentication should be avoided.

entries.name: Keycloak
entries.summary: Open source identity and access management: single sign-on, identity brokering, LDAP and Active Directory federation, over OpenID Connect, OAuth 2.0 and SAML 2.0.

cncf.text: Keycloak was accepted to CNCF on April 10, 2023 at the Incubating maturity level.

version.name: Keycloak
version.docs: keycloak.org docs index (shows 26.8.1) and the Server Administration guide (latest)

compare.text: Keycloak is a full identity server with its own user store, consoles and brokering. Dex is a small OIDC front for other identity providers.
Both are self-hosted identity servers. Keycloak is a CNCF incubating project.

notes: Start date is the repository creation date. The oldest GitHub release is 12.0.0 (2020-12-17); earlier releases are not on GitHub.
The home page and the docs index do not state a licence. Apache-2.0 is the SPDX id GitHub reports.
The server admin guide is 688,175 characters; only the first 100,000 were read.

sections.title: What it does
items: Single sign-on: users log in once through Keycloak, and one logout ends their sessions across the connected apps.
Standard protocols: OpenID Connect, OAuth 2.0 and SAML 2.0.
Identity brokering and social login: add social networks or connect external OpenID Connect or SAML identity providers from the admin console, with no application code change.
User federation: built in support for LDAP and Active Directory, and custom providers for other stores. A Kerberos bridge authenticates users already logged in to a Kerberos server.
Fine-grained authorization: policy-based permissions beyond role-based, managed in the admin console.

sections.title: Concepts
items: Realm: manages a set of users, credentials, roles and groups. Realms are isolated, so each one only manages and authenticates its own users.
Client: an entity that can ask Keycloak to authenticate a user, usually an application or service.
Users have attributes and can belong to groups and hold roles. A group can carry attributes and role mappings that its members inherit.
Authentication flows: the steps a user completes at login, registration or credential reset. A login flow can say which credential types are required.

sections.title: Consoles and API
items: Admin console: central management of server features, brokering, federation, applications, authorization policies, users and sessions.
Account console: users manage their profile, passwords, two-factor authentication, sessions, account history and linked identity providers.
Admin REST API and JavaDoc are published with the docs.

sections.title: Running it
items: The documentation index lists the guides Getting Started, Server Installation and Configuration, Server Container Image, Securing Applications and Services, Server Administration, Server Developer, Authorization Services, Upgrading and Release Notes.
Configuration is by guide. See Argo CD and Kubernetes for how Argo CD and the Kubernetes API server trust it.

entries.name: Dex
entries.summary: An OpenID Connect identity service that fronts other identity providers through connectors (LDAP, GitHub, SAML, OIDC and more). Argo CD can bundle it.

cncf.text: Dex was accepted to CNCF on June 25, 2020 at the Sandbox maturity level.

compare.text: Dex has no user management of its own beyond a local connector. Keycloak is a full identity server.

notes: Start date is the first GitHub release. The CNCF page also lists a first commit of July 25, 2016 from LFX Insights, which does not match; the date is unconfirmed.
The docs page read does not mention Helm or other install methods.

sections.title: What it is
items: Dex "is an identity service that uses OpenID Connect to drive authentication for other apps". It acts as a portal to other identity providers through connectors.

Connectors listed in the docs: LDAP, GitHub, SAML 2.0, GitLab, OpenID Connect, OAuth 2.0, Google, LinkedIn, Microsoft, AuthProxy, Bitbucket Cloud, a built in local connector, OpenShift, Atlassian Crowd, Gitea and OpenStack Keystone.
Storage backends shown in the architecture diagram: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, etcd, Kubernetes and in memory.

sections.title: Where it is used
items: Argo CD bundles Dex for providers that are not OIDC (SAML, LDAP) and configures it with dex.config in argocd-cm.
Argo CD architecture notes say Dex keeps its data in memory, so several instances can disagree.

entries.name: authentik
entries.summary: A self-hosted identity provider and SSO platform. Providers for OAuth2/OIDC, SAML, LDAP, SCIM, proxy and RADIUS. Open core: an enterprise edition adds features.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

entries.license: MIT (with an enterprise directory under a separate licence)
notes: GitHub reports NOASSERTION. The LICENSE says content outside the authentik/enterprise directory and the website directory is MIT, and the enterprise directory has its own licence.
Start date is the first GitHub release. The GitHub repository was created on 2019-12-30.

sections.title: What it is
items: An identity provider (IdP) and single sign-on platform. Three consoles: the flow interface (login steps run as stages), the user interface (a list of apps) and the admin interface.

Providers: OAuth2 and OIDC, SAML, SCIM, LDAP, Proxy (authentication in front of apps without SSO), RADIUS, Remote Access Control, WS-Federation, and integrations for Microsoft Entra ID and Google Workspace.
Installation: Docker Compose or Kubernetes.
An open source version is free. An Enterprise version adds a support centre and more features.

entries.name: Authelia
entries.summary: A 2FA and SSO authentication server that extends reverse proxies. Also an OpenID Connect provider.

started.basis: First GitHub release v4.0.0-alpha2 (the repository was created 2016-12-07)

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

notes: The introduction page does not say whether it forwards authentication, which user backends it supports, or its licence. Apache-2.0 is the SPDX id GitHub reports. The OpenID certification claim is GitHub's repository description, not checked on the certification list (unconfirmed).

sections.title: What it is
items: "A 2FA and SSO authentication server" that extends reverse proxies with authentication features.

Features named on the page: several two-factor methods, identity verification when registering a second factor, self-service password reset, and regulation that bans accounts after repeated failed attempts.
The docs sidebar lists Access Control, OpenID Connect 1.0, Trusted Headers SSO, Supported Proxies and authentication methods. GitHub's description says it is OpenID Certified.

entries.name: ZITADEL
entries.summary: Identity infrastructure with first-class multi-tenancy. OIDC, SAML and OAuth2 single sign-on. Self-hosted or ZITADEL Cloud.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

notes: The licence is AGPL-3.0 per the repository's LICENSE file, which matters for products that embed it. The docs home does not state it.
The docs page does not mention SCIM or LDAP (unconfirmed whether it supports them).

sections.title: What it is
items: "The Identity Infrastructure for Developers": a turnkey authentication and authorization service you can extend.
Single sign-on over OIDC, SAML and OAuth2. First-class multi-tenancy, with branding customisation and self-service.
ZITADEL Cloud is a public cloud service with a free tier. Self-hosted gives full control.

entries.name: Ory Hydra
entries.summary: An OpenID Certified OpenID Connect and OAuth2 provider that plugs into your own user management through headless APIs.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

notes: The Ory welcome page read does not describe Hydra, Keto, Oathkeeper or Polis, so the product descriptions come from the GitHub repository descriptions (unconfirmed beyond that).

sections.title: What it is
items: Per GitHub's description: an OpenID Certified OpenID Connect and OAuth2.1 provider written in Go, integrating with your user management through headless APIs. Self-host it or use Ory Network.
Ory also offers Ory Kratos for identity management. Ory Open Source, Ory Network (managed cloud) and an Ory Enterprise License are the three ways to run Ory.

entries.name: Ory Kratos
entries.summary: Headless authentication and identity management written in Go: login, registration, MFA, passkeys and social sign-in, with no built in UI.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

notes: Feature list is the GitHub repository description, not checked against the docs (unconfirmed).

sections.title: What it is
items: Per GitHub's description: headless, cloud native authentication and identity management written in Go, with passkeys, social sign-in, OIDC, magic link, multi-factor, SMS, SAML and TOTP.
Pair it with Ory Hydra when you also need to act as an OAuth2 or OpenID Connect provider.

entries.name: Casdoor
entries.summary: An open source identity and access management server with a web UI. Its repository describes OAuth, OIDC, SAML, CAS, LDAP, SCIM and WebAuthn support.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

notes: Read from the GitHub description only. The docs site redirects (casdoor.org to casdoor.ai) and was not read (unconfirmed).

sections.title: What it is
items: Per GitHub's description: an open source IAM and auth server with a web UI, supporting OAuth, OIDC, SAML, CAS, LDAP, SCIM, WebAuthn, TOTP and MFA.

entries.name: SimpleSAMLphp
entries.summary: A PHP application that does SAML authentication, as a service provider or an identity provider.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

notes: Only the GitHub description was read. That it targets SAML 2.0 is the project's well known use, not on the page read (unconfirmed).

sections.title: What it is
items: Per GitHub's description: "an application written in native PHP that deals with authentication". Its best known use is SAML 2.0, as an identity provider or service provider.

entries.name: LDAP
entries.summary: A protocol for reading and changing a directory of users, groups and other entries, and for checking a password with a bind. The classic user store behind many logins.

cncf.text: Specified by the IETF, not a CNCF project.

notes: Default ports (389 and 636) were not on the pages read, so they are not stated here (unconfirmed). StartTLS details were cut off on the RFC page read.
RFC 4511 is dated June 2006 and obsoletes RFC 2251, RFC 2830 and RFC 3771. version.released is the first of that month.

sections.title: Data model
items: A directory is a database designed for searching and browsing. An entry is a set of attributes identified by a unique distinguished name (DN), for example uid=babs,ou=People,dc=example,dc=com.
Each attribute has a type (cn, mail) and one or more values. The objectClass attribute decides which attributes the entry must and may have, so it sets the schema rules.
Entries form a hierarchy, the directory information tree (DIT). The DN string format is in RFC 4514.

sections.title: Operations (RFC 4511)
items: Bind authenticates the client, unbind ends the session. Search reads entries by base object, scope and filter.

Add and delete work on leaf entries. Modify applies add, delete or replace changes atomically. Modify DN renames or moves an entry. Compare checks a value. Abandon stops an operation. Extended adds operations such as StartTLS.
Authentication on bind: simple (a password) or SASL. An empty name is an anonymous bind. Details are in RFC 4513.

sections.title: In practice
items: Applications and identity providers use a bind to check a password and a search to find a user and their groups. Keycloak and Dex can read users from LDAP.
Common result codes: success (0), noSuchObject (32), invalidCredentials (49), insufficientAccessRights (50), unwillingToPerform (53).

entries.name: Kerberos
entries.summary: Ticket based network authentication: a user authenticates once, gets tickets, and Kerberos-aware services accept them without asking for the password again.

started.basis: Not stated on the page read

cncf.text: MIT project, not a CNCF project.

version.name: MIT Kerberos user docs
version.docs: web.mit.edu krb5-latest, read on 2026-10-26; no version shown on the page

notes: The page read does not define the KDC, TGT, service tickets or keytabs, so those are not described here (unconfirmed).
Licence is not stated on the page read. Start date and current release version are also not stated, so version shows the docs page date.

sections.title: Concepts
items: A principal is a Kerberos name with a primary (user or service), an optional instance and a realm, for example jennifer/admin. Realms are conventionally upper case.
After authenticating you get an initial ticket, an encrypted message that proves who you are. Tickets expire, and some can be renewed with kinit -R or forwarded to another host.
kinit gets tickets and kdestroy deletes them.

sections.title: In this topic
items: FreeIPA bundles MIT Kerberos as its key distribution centre. Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides managed Kerberos and NTLM for legacy apps.
Keycloak can bridge Kerberos: users already logged in to a Kerberos server are authenticated automatically.

entries.name: OpenLDAP
entries.summary: The open source LDAP directory server (slapd) and client libraries.

started.basis: Not stated on the pages read

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

version.name: OpenLDAP
version.docs: openldap.org release page and admin guide 2.6

notes: The GitHub repository is a mirror and publishes no releases, so versions and dates come from the openldap.org release page and the tag dates in the mirror (2026-10-21).
Whether 2.6 is a long-term release line is not stated on the pages read (unconfirmed).

sections.title: What it is
items: slapd, the standalone LDAP daemon, is a lightweight X.500-style directory server. It does not implement X.500 DAP. It supports LDAPv3 over IPv4, IPv6 and Unix IPC, plus SASL and TLS.
Released under the OpenLDAP Public License version 2.8 (17 August 2003), a permissive licence.
The release page lists 2.7.2 as a feature release and 2.6.16 documents.

entries.name: FreeIPA
entries.summary: An integrated identity and authentication system for Linux and UNIX networks: LDAP directory, Kerberos, certificate authority and DNS in one server, with a web UI and the ipa CLI.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

version.name: FreeIPA
version.docs: freeipa.org About page; version is the latest tag

notes: The About page does not state the licence, the platforms or the relation to Red Hat Identity Management. GPL-3.0 is the SPDX id GitHub reports.
The GitHub mirror has no releases. The version is the latest release-4-13-x tag and its tag date.

sections.title: Components
items: 389 Directory Server: the main data store, a multi-master LDAPv3 directory.
MIT Kerberos: the key distribution centre that provides single sign-on.
Dogtag Certificate System: an integrated CA and RA for certificate management.
DNS (optional, ISC BIND) and SSSD on the client side.

sections.title: Use
items: Provides centralised authentication, authorization and account information for users, groups and hosts. Administered from a web UI or the ipa command line tool. Several servers can join a domain for redundancy.

entries.name: Microsoft Entra ID
entries.summary: Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service, the directory behind Microsoft 365 and Azure. Free, P1 and P2 licences.

started.basis: Not stated on the page read

cncf.text: Commercial service, not a CNCF project.

notes: Included because you asked for the major cloud identity services; it is not open source. What the Free licence includes, the supported protocols and the rename from Azure Active Directory are not on the page read (unconfirmed).
Version is the page's updated_at date, since the service has no version number.

sections.title: What it is
items: Microsoft Entra ID is a cloud based identity and access management service that provides authentication, policy enforcement and protection for users, devices, apps and resources.

Every Microsoft 365, Azure or Dynamics CRM Online subscriber already has an Entra tenant. Licences: Entra ID Free, P1, P2, the Suite, and standalone products such as ID Governance, External ID and Workload ID.
Microsoft Entra Domain Services is a separate product that gives managed group policy, LDAP and Kerberos/NTLM for legacy apps.
Administer with the Entra admin center or Microsoft Graph. Build apps against the Microsoft identity platform.

entries.name: Google Cloud Identity
entries.summary: Google's identity as a service: manages users and groups, and federates with other identity providers such as Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID.

started.basis: Not stated on the page read

cncf.text: Commercial service, not a CNCF project.

notes: The overview page does not describe the Free and Premium editions, SAML or OIDC single sign-on, LDAP, SCIM, or the relation to Google Workspace (unconfirmed).

sections.title: What it is
items: "An Identity as a Service (IDaaS) solution that centrally manages users and groups." You create a Cloud Identity account for each user and group, then use IAM to control access to Google Cloud resources.

It can federate identities between Google and other providers such as Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID, and manage every account in your domain, including personal accounts like Gmail that would otherwise be outside your control.

entries.name: AWS IAM Identity Center
entries.summary: AWS's workforce SSO: connect your identity provider or create users, then give them access to AWS accounts and AWS managed applications.

started.basis: Renamed from AWS Single Sign-On on this date; the earlier start is unconfirmed

cncf.text: Commercial service, not a CNCF project.

version.name: AWS IAM Identity Center
version.docs: docs.aws.amazon.com singlesignon user guide, no version or date on page

notes: The page read does not state a price, and does not mention SCIM. Cost is unconfirmed here.
The 2022-07-26 date is the rename, not the first release.

sections.title: What it is
items: "The AWS solution for connecting your workforce users to AWS managed applications and other AWS resources." You can connect an existing identity provider and synchronise users and groups, or create users in IAM Identity Center.
One point of federation: with a SAML 2.0 identity provider you federate once and manage one certificate.

Two instance types: organization instances (the only ones that manage access to AWS accounts, recommended for production) and account instances (for isolated deployments of select managed applications).
On July 26, 2022, AWS Single Sign-On was renamed to AWS IAM Identity Center. The sso and identitystore API names are unchanged.

entries.name: Argo CD and Kubernetes
entries.summary: How a platform trusts your identity provider: Argo CD with the built in Dex or a direct OIDC provider, and the Kubernetes API server with OIDC tokens.

cncf.text: Documentation topic.

version.name: Argo CD docs (stable) and Kubernetes authentication docs

notes: The Kubernetes page was read from the HTML for the flags table and the OIDC section. How kubectl runs a credential plugin and the stable state of AuthenticationConfiguration were not confirmed from the page (unconfirmed). kubelogin's own description is from its GitHub repository (Apache-2.0, latest v1.36.4 on 2026-09-08).
Argo CD pages carry no version. They are the stable docs read when the latest release was v3.5.6.

sections.title: Argo CD: choose a path
items: Built in admin user: full access, for the first setup only. Disable it with admin.enabled "false" in argocd-cm.
Local users: accounts.<name> in argocd-cm with capability apiKey (tokens) or login (UI). Each needs RBAC rules or falls back to policy.default. The docs recommend SSO for larger teams.
Bundled Dex: for providers that are not OIDC (SAML, LDAP) or to use Dex connector features. Set dex.config in argocd-cm.
Existing OIDC provider directly: set oidc.config in argocd-cm with issuer, clientID and clientSecret.

sections.title: Argo CD with Keycloak (from the Argo CD guide)
items: Keycloak client: with the client secret method turn client authentication on. For PKCE set the PKCE method to S256.
Valid redirect URIs: https://<hostname>/auth/callback, http://localhost:8085/auth/callback for the CLI (it must match --sso-port), and https://<hostname>/pkce/verify for the UI with PKCE.

Store the secret in argocd-secret as oidc.keycloak.clientSecret. In oidc.config set name, issuer (https://keycloak.example.com/realms/master, with /auth for Keycloak older than 17), clientID, clientSecret ($oidc.keycloak.clientSecret), requestedScopes including groups and offline_access, and refreshTokenThreshold.
Groups: create a client scope named groups with a Group Membership mapper whose token claim name is groups, with the full group path turned off, and add it to the client as a default scope.
CLI login with PKCE: argocd login <server> --sso --grpc-web.

sections.title: Argo CD RBAC
items: Global RBAC lives in argocd-rbac-cm. Built in roles: role:readonly and role:admin. Project roles are in each AppProject's spec.roles.

policy.csv: p, <role/user/group>, <resource>, <action>, <object>, <effect> and g, <user/group>, <role>. A matching deny wins over any allow. A group's p policies only apply once the group is given a role with g.
Map an SSO group to a role, for example g, ArgoCDAdmins, role:admin. The scopes setting names which claims are checked for groups, and defaults to groups.
policy.default is the role for every authenticated user and a deny cannot block it, so the docs recommend a minimal role. Test with argocd admin settings rbac validate and rbac can.

sections.title: Kubernetes API server
items: Kubernetes has no user objects and no web login. Normal users come from outside, for example a client certificate signed by the cluster CA (the username is the common name). Kubernetes does not provide an OpenID Connect identity provider: bring your own.
The identity provider must support OIDC discovery, because the API server finds the signing keys from the issuer. The API server uses the id_token, not the access token, as the bearer token.

Flags: --oidc-issuer-url (https only, required), --oidc-client-id (required), --oidc-username-claim, --oidc-username-prefix, --oidc-groups-claim (an array of strings), --oidc-groups-prefix, --oidc-required-claim.
Instead of flags, --authentication-config points to an AuthenticationConfiguration file, which allows several authenticators and several audiences per issuer.
kubectl does not log you in itself. kubelogin (kubectl oidc-login) is a kubectl plugin for OIDC authentication.
